Results: We present The Little Scientist, a framework that maps the scientific method onto an LLM agent in a loop: a Scientist agent iterates hypothesis, prediction, code, test, and reconciliation inside an evaluation environment that returns structured diagnostics, and a Kuhn agent injects paradigm-shifting reframings at plateaus. On DNA motif discovery, the process wrote an algorithm from scratch (DALE) that outperforms STREME across 132 ENCODE transcription factors on the shuffled-negative benchmark (mean AUROC 0.842 vs. 0.803) while running 11x faster. We then asked why this method worked, and that question became the paper's scientific core: a preregistered, controlled teardown of the framework's own scaffolding consisting of ten ablation arms against one-shot bandit nulls. The answer overturned the premise. Seven of ten loop arms fail to beat a bandit drawing samples from the same model and prompt, the full scaffold performs below blind sampling at 7-8x the token cost, and a floor-prompt arm with no framework at all wins on both score and value per token. On a held-out genomic benchmark, the best loop artifact and the best bandit draw agree to within 0.002, and the DALE algorithm from the initial experiment scored similarly. The convergent picture is that LLM agents do not reason their way past what training placed in the weights. Autoresearch, on this evidence, is sampling, selection, and remixing, which is the bet the Evolve-family architectures made when they chose populations and external selection over scratchpad reasoning, and why those choices were right.

Multiagent Systems.title: Decision Models as Scalable Economic Surrogates that Capture Human Variation
Multiagent Systems.summary: Decision Models (DMs), a new class of AI models, give fast responses and return a probability distribution over a fixed set of options. These properties make them candidate human surrogates in economic simulations and surveys, a role increasingly filled by Large Language Models (LLMs), which are costly at scale and under-represent the variation in human behaviour. We present a first evaluation of DMs as human surrogates in economics, comparing 10 DMs with 8 LLMs in three economic settings: a household spending survey on consumption, several classic economic games and a labour-market field experiment. Frontier DMs, those that score highest on general decision-making benchmarks, reproduce the variation in human responses more closely than LLMs in all three settings. They capture the modal human response as well as LLMs in the spending survey, but less well in the economic games. Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

Multiagent Systems.title: MA-SafeDiffuser: Safe Multi-Agent Planning with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
Multiagent Systems.summary: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at AAMAS 2026. 14 pages, including supplementary material

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Dexterous In-Hand Object Pose Reaching with Learned Safety Filters
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 26 pages, 30 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Iterative Methods for Solving Feedback-Type Linear Equations under Small Phase Condition
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper investigates iterative methods for solving feedback-type linear equations under small phase condition. We first develop an iterative solution scheme for linear equations with sectorial (semi-sectorial) matrices, i.e., matrices whose numerical ranges are contained in an open (closed) half complex plane. Exploiting the geometric properties of the numerical range, we introduce the notion of numerical-radius contraction as a convergence criterion. Such a scheme, with some extra effort, leads to an iterative method for the feedback-type equations under small phase condition, whose convergence condition is characterized in terms of phase information. This complements classical iterative methods for feedback-type equations based on the small gain condition. A case study on large-scale power networks is presented to illustrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Safe Navigation in Cluttered Environments Via Spline-Based Harmonic Potential Fields
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We provide a motion-planning framework for target reaching and obstacle avoidance in cluttered environments. Given a polyhedral decomposition of the feasible space, the agent is guided through a prescribed sequence of cells by a suitable control policy. For each cell, we construct a potential induced by a harmonic function on the unit disk whose Dirichlet boundary condition is represented by a cardinal B-spline curve. A detailed analysis of the curve periodicity, support, and control-point selection provides an explicit analytical construction of these potentials and the associated vector fields. We further characterize inter-cell control continuity and forward invariance of non-exit facets, and introduce a smoothed control law ensuring continuous switching between independently constructed neighboring cells. Numerical results illustrate that the resulting framework safely guides the agent along the prescribed cell sequence from the initial point to the target.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: The Novelty Horizon H_N: Why Large Language Models Fail to Generate Scientific Data beyond Their Training Distribution
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) lack physical grounding and extrapolation. This paper formalises the Novelty Horizon as tasks needing extrapolation beyond training support, causal reasoning absent from learned correlations, or post-frontier information. A forensic analysis tests LLMs on unguided, guided, and ground-truth data from an underrepresented diode-clamped short-circuit experiment using temporal, spectral, and statistical validation against a first-principles Modified Ohm's Law. Both script-based approaches fail catastrophically with physical and spectral inconsistencies, extreme statistical pathologies, zero Generative Fidelity Score, and linear-regime outputs. Direct prompting corroborates distinct failure modes. This paper introduces the Past Information Boundary and physics-based authentication. LLM data generation cannot extrapolate past the Novelty Horizon essential for novel discovery. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems must preserve human causal reasoning and experimental design.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Towards an Optimal Control Foundation of Early Exits - Turnpikes and ResNets
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The feed-forward propagation through neural networks is crucial for training and inference. To trade off efficiency and accuracy, it has been proposed to consider intermediate outputs of hidden states as data-dependent regularization during training and, ultimately, as early-exits during inference. In this work, we analyze the joint optimization of loss functions computed for the output layer and intermediate layers using optimal control theory. We prove that ResNets trained in this joint fashion exhibit the so-called turnpike phenomenon, this implies that the number of layers required to reach a prescribed loss level is bounded from above independently of the overall network depth. This induces a similarity property across the internal representations of early-exiting networks of varying depths. We connect the turnpike to the overthinking phenomenon, and provide theoretical insights into the success of early-exit criteria derived from softmax probabilities, specifically entropy and max-probability. In a range of experiments, we demonstrate the existence and effect of turnpikes and the resulting similarity in the early-exit performance for ResNets of varying depths.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Capability-Aware Heterogeneous Control Barrier Functions for Decentralized Multi-Robot Safe Navigation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Safe decentralized navigation in heterogeneous robot teams is challenging because robots with different dynamics and control limits cannot satisfy identical collision-avoidance obligations equally well. Existing methods often rely on model-specific safety formulations or allocate avoidance responsibility without considering whether the assigned control is physically realizable, possibly leading to safety-constrained QP infeasibility and safety violations. We propose Capability-Aware Heterogeneous Control Barrier Functions (CA-HCBF), a decentralized framework for consistent safety enforcement and capability-aware responsibility allocation. We derive a unified operational-space second-order control-affine formulation for holonomic and nonholonomic mobile robots through canonical transformation and backstepping, addressing the relative-degree mismatch while preserving forward invariance of the pairwise safe set. Second, we quantify each robot's achievable control authority along the safety-critical direction using a support-function-based capability metric and use it to distribute pairwise avoidance responsibility. A feasibility-aware clipping mechanism further mitigates physically unrealizable responsibility assignments. Simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and hardware experiments demonstrate high task completion with low safety violations and reduction in local QP infeasibility.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Stray Losses in Power Transformers: A Comparative Study of Modeling Frameworks for Mild Steel
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Accurately predicting eddy-current and hysteresis losses in mild steel components such as the structural parts and tank of power transformers remains a challenge in transformer design. Conventional numerical approaches for eddy-current loss analysis require discretization at a fraction of the skin depth. While accurate, such fine volumetric mesh becomes computationally prohibitive for large power transformers. Moreover, hysteresis loss is not always included in this analysis. To investigate the trade-off between computational cost and accuracy, this work presents a comparative analysis of eight distinct modeling frameworks for predicting both eddy-current and hysteresis losses in mild steel. These include efficient methods avoiding meshing, such as standard impedance boundary conditions, and more accurate approaches retaining full volumetric meshing, namely complex permeability, nonlinear single-valued B-H curve, and Jiles-Atherton hysteresis modeling. To accurately represent the material's electromagnetic behavior, the properties of the mild steel used are measured directly from samples. Finally, loss measurements are conducted to benchmark all eight frameworks, demonstrating mean absolute percentage errors between predictions and measurements generally below 20%.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 13 pages, 18 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Magnetics

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Graph-Based Dynamic Activity Prediction for Real-Time Power System Applications
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Online dynamic security assessment and day-ahead planning require rapid identification of where disturbances will produce significant dynamic activity. Full time-domain simulations are computationally demanding, while existing machine-learning approaches predict system-level outcomes or require post-disturbance trajectories. This paper proposes a pair-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge features (GINE) framework comprising two task-specific models for predicting bus-voltage and generator apparent-power activity from the operating point and contingency description. Physically aware KPI cuts convert simulated responses into ordinal activity targets for model training. Evaluations on Nordic 32 and the French transmission system with more than 6 000 buses show that pair-aware fusion and graph embeddings improve on a local baseline on Nordic 32, with GINE the lower-cost graph encoder, and that the framework remains effective at large scale. As a downstream application, the predicted activity maps guide Adaptive Model Simplification, reducing continuous and discrete model variables by 72% and 66%, achieving speedups of up to 3.16x, and preserving voltage trajectories when critical substations are retained. These results demonstrate scalable, pre-disturbance prediction of component-level dynamic activity.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 3 figures; submitted to the invited session "Learning and identification of port-Hamiltonian systems" at the 21st IFAC Symposium on System Identification (SYSID 2027)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Modern unit commitment (UC) scenarios, particularly those involving uncertainties from demand fluctuations and renewable energy sources, pose significant challenges to traditional optimization methods due to the large search spaces they encompass. This paper proposes a quantum computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic UC, integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers across test systems, including the IEEE 118-bus system. A novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) reformulation accommodates generator scaling and 24-hour scheduling horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints. A divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation address scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, reducing compilation time by up to two orders of magnitude. Experimental results demonstrate the pipeline's ability to achieve efficient, scalable, and accurate UC optimization under uncertainty: the hybrid quantum method approach matches the classical baseline, reduces stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours, and characterizes pure quantum annealing as limited to small systems with 0.22% to 2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations. These results provide an analysis of the scalability and computational practicality of hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling in UC.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. 17 pages

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Two-Player Zero-Sum Hybrid Games with Set-Valued Dynamics
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In this paper, we formulate a two-player zero-sum game under dynamic constraints defined in terms of a hybrid inclusion. The game consists of a min-max problem involving a cost functional that depends on the actions and corresponding (potentially non-unique) solutions, defined as functions of hybrid time and, hence, can flow or jump. We present sufficient conditions given in terms of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs-like equations to establish a bound and to exactly evaluate the worst-case cost under the optimal strategy. Under additional conditions, we show that the proposed optimal state-feedback laws render a set of interest pre-asymptotically stable for the resulting hybrid closed-loop system. The results are illustrated in an application with sporadic jumps and linear quadratic hybrid dynamics.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: From Roadside Sensing to Risk-Informed Safety Control: Surrogate Safety Measures as a Cyber-Physical Interface
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Proactive intersection safety analysis depends on trajectory data whose reliability varies by sensing modality, yet infrastructure-perception and surrogate safety measure (SSM) research have only recently begun to converge. This paper synthesizes both literatures alongside control theory to clarify how sensing choices, safety metrics, and predictive control connect end-to-end, and where infrastructure-derived risk signals could inform autonomous vehicle decision-making. Searches covered light detection and ranging (LiDAR), cooperative perception, time-to-collision (TTC), post-encroachment time (PET), extreme value theory, model predictive control (MPC), and signal control. Screening considered trajectory-based safety and control relevance, excluding detection benchmarks without safety linkage. This structured narrative synthesis retained 56 sources. No single SSM is universally valid: one-dimensional TTC and modified TTC suit longitudinal conflicts, two-dimensional TTC extends time-based measurement to crossing geometries, and observed PET captures crossing and vulnerable road user (VRU) conflicts but only after the event. LiDAR consistently outperforms camera-only sensing for continuous three-dimensional trajectory extraction, illumination robustness, and privacy, though its range degrades in heavy rain, fog, and snow. Its output becomes control-ready only when paired with filtering--Kalman, Savitzky-Golay--that stabilizes noisy detections. This review complements it from the infrastructure side: it examines how roadside sensing affects that chain's reliability, classifies SSMs by conflict geometry and temporal availability, and maps risk components onto control objectives and constraints for infrastructure and connected and automated vehicle (CAV) applications.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Caging Vision-Language Navigation for Legged Robots via Barrier-Certified Safety Architecture
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Matrix-Separation Approach for Stability of Discrete-Time Systems with Time-Varying Delay
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This letter addresses the stability analysis of discrete-time linear systems with time-varying delay using a Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional (LKF) framework. An improved matrix-separation-based inequality (IMSBI) is developed to obtain tighter bounds for the summation terms arising in the forward difference of the LKF. Based on this result, an augmented LKF incorporating additional cross-terms is constructed to capture the interaction between system states and delay evolution. This leads to a less conservative delay-dependent stability criterion expressed as linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). Numerical results demonstrate improved stability margins and a reduced number of decision variables compared with existing methods.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: On the Convexity of Common Resource Adequacy and Capacity Accreditation Metrics
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Many emerging capacity expansion optimization formulations implicitly presume the convexity (or concavity) of power system adequacy risk (or capacity accreditation) metrics. These assumptions have yet to be formally justified. We present concise mathematical proofs validating the claim for certain metrics (expected unserved energy and effective load carrying capability), but also provide simple invalidating counterexamples for others (loss-of-load expectation and equivalent firm capacity). Formulations built on non-convex (non-concave) metrics structurally undervalue candidate portfolio adequacy, and so cannot claim to produce least-cost expansion plans.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Sufficient and Necessary Smooth Barrier-Like Conditions for Continuous-Time Finite-Horizon Safety Verification
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study finite-horizon safety verification for continuous-time stochastic systems modeled by stochastic differential equations. Given an open and bounded safe set, a compact initial set, a finite time horizon, and a prescribed violation-probability threshold, the objective is to certify that the exit probability from the safe set before the horizon remains below the threshold. Under uniform ellipticity of the diffusion matrix and regularity of the safe-set boundary, we develop a time-dependent barrier-like condition expressed as a set of functional inequalities, obtained by relaxing a parabolic initial-boundary value problem associated with the exit probability. If a function satisfies the condition, then the probability of leaving the safe set before the horizon is guaranteed to remain below the threshold. Conversely, when the exit probability is strictly smaller than the prescribed threshold uniformly over the initial set, the barrier-like condition is also necessary: there exists a smooth function satisfying it. Furthermore, when the dynamics are polynomial and the set descriptions are semialgebraic, the problem of verifying the condition admits a sum-of-squares formulation that is both sound and complete, yielding a complete degree hierarchy for finite-horizon stochastic safety verification.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: LQG solution for POMDP without estimating states: A minimum variance approach
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper investigates the control of discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems subject to incomplete and corrupted measurements. Specifically, we focus on designing a Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controller without relying on explicit state estimation. By leveraging minimum variance duality, our approach allows the current control input to be represented as a linear function of available measurements and previously applied inputs, successfully reducing the task to a tractable deterministic optimization problem. We provide theoretical justification for this framework and demonstrate its practical effectiveness through numerical experiments.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Assignment-Free Swarm Navigation via Adaptive Target-Field Planning and Mean-Shift Exploration
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Mean-shift exploration enables assignment-free swarm shape assembly, but obstacle-constrained navigation additionally requires coordinated adaptation of the desired morphology and its physical execution. This paper presents an environment-adaptive navigation framework that integrates target-field planning, execution regulation, and morphology-preserving mean-shift exploration. A feasibility-aware graph search plans the position, orientation, and morphology of an unlabeled target field without specifying robot-specific goals. An execution-regulated reference manager adjusts field progression and morphology switching using swarm entering, coverage, and lag metrics. A moving-frame controller separates prescribed rigid motion from local mean-shift redistribution and incorporates neighbor interactions and obstacle responses. Simulations and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework coordinates morphology transitions and collective motion for assignment-free swarm navigation through cluttered environments.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Training Specialist LLMs on Your Phone: Forward-Only Optimization via Block-Spectral Coordinates
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: TriMedium: A Cross-Medium Simulator for Embodied Networking Across Air-Ground-Sea
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Embodied intelligent applications have expanded from air and ground into maritime environments, where missions such as coastal reporting require coordination among underwater sensing, surface gateways, and aerial relays. Yet field trials remain costly, and existing simulation tools make it difficult to study how cross-medium communication affects cooperation among these platforms. We present TriMedium, an integrated Air-Ground-Sea simulator for cross-medium embodied networking. TriMedium has three design elements. First, it provides a shared three-dimensional world where aerial, terrestrial, and underwater entities coexist, so underwater agent motion and visual observations stay geometrically consistent with air and ground nodes. Second, it uses a common simulation clock that preserves observation timestamps while scheduling delayed communication and computation, clarifying when the shore receiver obtains each observation. Third, modular quantization and compression interfaces accommodate heterogeneous telemetry and image pipelines, while integrity checks separate intentional lossy distortion from incomplete or corrupted delivery. Three case studies validate TriMedium. Multimodal data delivery tests telemetry and image pipelines, scene construction examines cross-domain spatial consistency, and positioning assesses geometric accuracy under delayed communication. Together, they show TriMedium enables embodied networking by quantifying cross-medium delivery dynamics and fidelity across heterogeneous payloads.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Multi-experiment identification from short repeated transients:the human response to pushes in a Tai Chi posture
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The effect of Tai Chi postures on the mechanical response of the body to external pushes is usually assessed with clinical balance scores, which say little about the underlying dynamics. We identify, for five subjects and eight postural conditions, linear models from the mechanical work transferred by a pendulum hitting the forearm to the change of the antero-posterior ground reaction force. Each trial contains 10 to 16 impacts, and each impact yields a transient of 0.55\,s only. Building on earlier analyses of these data, we improve the processing chain in three ways. The input is related to the energy lost by the pendulum and its repeatability is quantified. The output is defined component-wise, which makes it independent of the zeroing of the force plate. Finally, the impacts are stacked in a multi-experiment least-squares problem and validated on unseen impacts. Tenth-order ARX models then reach a median leave-one-impact-out fit of 65\%, against 72\% for the repeatability of the response itself, and never require stability enforcement, unlike estimation on averaged impacts. Closing the eyes lengthens the identified delay by about 70\,ms in all subjects, and the Tai Chi posture increases the antero-posterior force transmitted per joule in four of five subjects. Surface EMG envelopes show a tonic co-activation of the lower-leg muscles in this posture, a smaller reactive triceps burst and a fast habituation of the tibialis response. Together, they point to a stiffer, anticipatory postural strategy.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, October 2026

Systems and Control (EESS).title: TuneBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Power System Dynamic Model Calibration
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can automate complex engineering workflows by interacting with tools, interpreting feedback, and making iterative decisions. This paper introduces TuneBench, a benchmark for evaluating Agentic AI in power system dynamic model calibration, where controller parameters are adjusted to reproduce target dynamic responses. The benchmark reflects a common Transmission System Operator (TSO) practice, in which equivalent models used for Dynamic Security Assessment (DSA) are calibrated against measurements from grid-code compliance tests when proprietary models are unavailable. Two cases of increasing complexity are considered: the governor and Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) of a synchronous generator and the control system of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), both tuned against active-power and voltage step tests within a budget of 15 simulations. LLM-based agents are compared with random search and Genetic Algorithm (GA) baselines over 10 independent runs. Only the most advanced models, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6, accurately reproduce all target trajectories, with median R2 above 0.995 in every test and tracking errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than the baselines. The agent logs show that these agents autonomously extract dynamic performance indices, such as settling time and damping, and relate them to specific control parameters, decomposing the tuning problem into physically interpretable sub-problems. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/Power-Agent/PowerAgentBench/tree/main/benchmarks/dynamic/level3.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: On the IQC and SRG Frameworks: Equivalences and Converse Results
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) and scaled relative graphs (SRGs) are two prominent frameworks for analyzing feedback systems. Although both frameworks are rooted in the same graph separation principle, a general characterization of their relationship has remained unavailable. This paper establishes conditions under which the IQC- and SRG frameworks are equivalent. To this end, we introduce two new classes of systems, termed disjunctive and conjunctive systems, which are respectively characterized by unions and intersections of quadratic input-output constraints. Under structural assumptions, we prove equivalence between the IQC and SRG frameworks for these system classes. By exploiting this equivalence, we develop novel IQC- and SRG-based converse stability results for linear and nonlinear systems. Our results accommodate multiple quadratic constraints, extending well-known converse results in robust control beyond the single-constraint setting.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A research world model of power engineering learns its dynamics and reveals what-ifs
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Decisions about the direction of research in power engineering determine which technologies mature and, through them, shape infrastructure that lasts decades, yet their consequences cannot be observed before they are taken, and existing forecasts of research fields extrapolate a single trajectory. Here we introduce research world models, which treat a research field as a dynamical system that can be acted upon, and establish one for power engineering from 1.1 million papers. A distilled language model reads each paper into role-typed concepts, two sophisticated, high-fidelity graph-temporal neural network cores learn how the resulting concept network evolves, and operators learned from natural experiments in the publication record estimate the effects of interventions. In temporally held-out tests, the model forecast years ahead which concepts would grow and which method-target pairs would be joined for the first time, outperforming tuned machine-learning baselines in most settings, and its estimated intervention effects tracked those realized in natural experiments it had not seen. Its training scheme and three of its operators replicated in two fields withheld from development. Questions posed in natural language are compiled by a domain-specialized 27-billion-parameter language model into executable actions and answered as paired simulations with and without the intervention. The answers were rated 4.1 of 5 for faithfulness by an independent language-model judge. By revealing the latent dynamics of a research field and its response to interventions, research world models offer a new way to simulate and test research decisions before they are made.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
Systems and Control (EESS).summary:
Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories.
  More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense.
  In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Block Diagram Analysis of an Amplitude-Frequency Design Principle in Biological Oscillators
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: An important design principle for biological oscillators divides oscillators into two types: fixed frequency, variable amplitude and fixed amplitude, variable frequency. Because of the interplay of nonlinearity and feedback, both positive and negative, analytical investigations of this design principle are primarily based on numerical simulations of ordinary differential equations. To enhance the qualitative and quantitative characterization of this design principle, we adapted and developed a block diagram modeling framework. We showed how the observed amplitude-frequency characteristics could be obtained from the block diagram models of both the types of oscillators. We obtained explicit constraints on the positive feedback and negative feedback strengths for the oscillations to exist. We represented both types of oscillators in a single unifying, control-theoretic framework that connects both the types of oscillators under a single theoretical model. These results contribute to a systems and control perspective on oscillations in biology and related contexts.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Deep State-Space Model Compression Method using Upper Bound on Output Error
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study deep state-space models (Deep SSMs) that contain linear quadratic-output (LQO) systems as internal blocks and present a compression method with a provable output error guarantee. We first derive an upper bound on the output error between two Deep SSMs and show that the bound can be expressed in terms of the $h^2$-error norms between the layerwise LQO systems. In particular, we show that reducing the $h^2$ approximation errors of the LQO systems placed in shallow layers is effective in reducing the derived upper bound on the output error. Next, we formulate an optimization problem for the derived upper bound and develop a gradient-based MOR method. In the numerical experiments, using the IMDb task from the LRA benchmark, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed upper-bound-based compression method. In particular, we show that the number of trainable parameters can be reduced by approximately 60\% without retraining while maintaining the performance of the original model.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Supervised Residual NMPC in Force-Disturbed Quadrotors
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Residual deployment can affect closed-loop tracking. We compare two ways to deploy one supervised acceleration-residual network in nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) of a quadrotor. Cyclewise deployment repeats one correction across the horizon. Stagewise deployment evaluates shifted prediction nodes before the solve. Network parameters remain fixed during control. On prescribed force pulses, both schemes improve average tracking mainly after force removal, but worsen hover; some prediction checks also fail. Seed 1 reinforcement-learning benchmarks add no mean benefit under pulses or prescribed random forces. On 220 conditions, cyclewise and stagewise supervision reduce mean integral absolute position error (IAE) by 4.38% and 7.77%. On a separate 32-condition bank, fixed gain 1.5 lowers IAE by 27.47% relative to stagewise supervision but raises angular-rate root-mean-square error by 10.19%. In one synthetic computational fluid dynamics field, stagewise supervision lowers four-task mean IAE by 2.01% against a same-graph zero-residual control; some secondary metrics worsen. These simulations show that residual deployment affects tracking, with gains and limitations that depend on task and motion metric.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Co-Optimization of Network Topology and Variable Impedance Devices under Dynamic Line Ratings in Power Transmission Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Power system operators are increasingly deploying Grid Enhancing Technologies (GETs) to mitigate operational challenges such as line and transformer congestion, and voltage violations. These technologies, including Network Topology Optimization (NTO), Variable Impedance Devices (VIDs), and Dynamic Line Rating (DLR), enhance system flexibility and enable better utilization of existing network assets. However, as the deployment of multiple GETs grows, effective coordination among them becomes essential to fully realize their potential benefits. This paper presents a co-optimization framework that models and coordinates NTO, VID, and DLR within a unified optimization scheme to alleviate network congestion and minimize operational costs. The NTO formulation is developed using a node-breaker model, offering finer switching granularity and improved operational flexibility. The inclusion of VIDs introduces nonlinear and non-convex relationships in the optimization problem. DLR takes into account of weather conditions, primarily wind speed and ambient temperature, enabling adaptive utilization of transmission capacity. The proposed framework is validated on standard IEEE benchmark test systems, demonstrating its effectiveness under varying numbers and placements of impedance controllers.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: This paper has been withdrawn due to its similarity to another paper

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Automated consolidation of dispersed DSO data resources into a consistent digital twin of the distribution grid
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The energy transition causes a growing number of distributed flexible energy resources in the low voltage grid. To utilize that flexibility, automation and control algorithms are needed, which typically are developed in theoretical research. We build a cyberphysical algorithm test bed to bridge the gap between theoretical research and practical application in cooperation with a local DSO in Walenstadt, Switzerland. To obtain suitable monitoring and data analysis capabilities from their existing data landscape, we propose tool-independent data harmonization measures in preparation for a digital twin of the grid. For data extraction from high-security network zones we developed a secure pipeline that implements a logical data diode ensuring one-way traffic only. Furthermore, we established a test community of voluntary prosumer households, whose flexible assets were made accessible through a common backend, giving us actuation capabilities. The presented publish-subscribe architecture is not only suitable to integrate various data sources into a central data collection, but also to manage access privileges of different stakeholders. This could support unbundling of an organization's data flows and the implementation of data space concepts.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: WiSI: Wireless-in-the-Loop Self-Improvement
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The growing autonomy of AI agents has enabled self-improvement, where agents iteratively refine their programs through execution feedback and performance evaluation. As these agents increasingly operate in physical environments and rely on wireless connectivity, communication conditions become an integral part of their improvement process. However, existing approaches largely assume ideal communication, overlooking how wireless conditions shape both the feedback that guides program modifications and the evaluation outcomes that determine which modifications survive. This challenge is further complicated by the coupling between agent behavior and wireless connectivity, as agents influence their own communication conditions through mobility and transmission decisions. To address this problem, we propose WiSI, a wireless-in-the-loop self-improvement framework that integrates spatiotemporal wireless channels, edge-assisted perception, and Large Language Model-driven program improvement. By incorporating wireless execution into the improvement loop, WiSI reveals how wireless execution experience shapes the generation and retention of program structures, and investigates the wireless conditions needed for robust improvement. Experiments show that agents improved under ideal links achieve only 40.0% task success under congestion, compared with 77.2% when improved under realistic wireless conditions. More importantly, wireless-aware feedback and selection jointly enable agents to discover and retain communication-efficient program structures that outperform parameter tuning and remain robust even with inaccurate run-time channel observations. We further find that moderate-load or mixed-network evaluation maintains strong performance across deployment conditions, while simplified models preserving link-rate statistics achieve comparable results without detailed spatial channel information.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Competition, Switching, and Control in Coupled Adoption-Opinion Dynamics
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We propose a Multi-technology AdopTion-opinion co-Evolution (MATE) model to describe the diffusion of $m \geq 2$ competing alternatives within a networked population whose opinions evolve under social influence and the feedback generated by adoption. Communities interact through two layers: a physical network governing exposure to adoption, and a social network shaping opinion evolution through social imitation. Individuals can adopt a technology, eventually becoming dissatisfied at a rate reflecting the quality of the technology, and switch to an alternative at a rate driven by their opinion of that alternative. For an arbitrary number of competing technologies $m \geq 2$, we characterize the equilibria and establish the existence of an adoption-diffused equilibrium in which all technologies coexist. For $m > 2$, the equilibrium configuration depends on the broader competitive environment: unlike the two-technology case, within-community relative adoption generally depends also on equilibrium opinions and on the other alternatives. Finally, we formulate finite-horizon opinion-shaping control problems, derive necessary optimality conditions via the discrete-time Pontryagin maximum principle, and compute numerical extremals using a forward-backward sweep method.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Moving Horizon Estimation and Constrained Model Predictive Control for Balancing a Wheel-Legged Robot Under Unknown Disturbances
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Wheel-legged robots balance on two wheels while using articulated legs to change height, absorb impacts, and cross uneven terrain. On hardware, the balance controller must rely on noisy inertial and encoder measurements, and it must reject disturbances that are not known in advance, such as payloads and wind, without exceeding motor torque limits. This paper presents a moving horizon estimator (MHE) combined with an offset-free, constrained model predictive controller (MPC) for the sagittal balance of a 9.95 kg wheel-legged robot. The estimator uses a virtual-leg model augmented with a horizontal hip force, a body pitch torque, and a gyroscope bias. Its accelerometer model removes the predicted hip acceleration, and its process noise is increased when an impact is detected. We evaluate the approach in MuJoCo with simulated sensor noise, bias, quantization, and delay, and compare it with LQR baselines that use ground-truth state, a complementary filter, or the same MHE. In a driving, squatting, reversing, and bowing sequence, MPC with MHE reduced the RMS speed error to 0.11 m/s, compared with 0.24 m/s for LQR with ground-truth state. Under an unknown 2 kg payload and a 10 N headwind, the mean position error in wind was 6 cm, compared with 81 cm for LQR with ground-truth state. Across a 3 $\times$ 4 grid of payloads and headwinds, LQR with the same estimator fell in 3 of 12 combinations, compared with 1 of 12 for MPC. These results are limited to simulation on flat ground, and experimental validation on hardware remains future work.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Computing Invariant Reachable Sets through Sum-of-Squares Programming
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Funnels, time-varying invariant sets around nominal trajectories, certify that a closed-loop system tracks its plan, and can be composed into verified motion plans. Their computation by sum-of-squares (SOS) programming is well established in formulation but not in practice: the result depends on implementation choices such as the initial guess, Lyapunov function normalization, and termination rule, which the literature documents only briefly. This paper presents a self-contained treatment of SOS-based funnel computation, implemented in the open-source package computeSOSFunnels. We propose a minimum-volume formulation with inlet and outlet constraints under which funnels with coinciding nominal endpoints compose by construction. Numerical experiments on a unicycle, with timing studies on a cart-pole and a 12-state quadrotor, characterize the pipeline: infeasible initial guesses are partly decidable before solving, the certificate shows no violations among 39,000 boundary samples per funnel under the true dynamics, and constructing the semidefinite program, not solving it, dominates computation time.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology. Code: github.com/khalid2696/computeSOSFunnels

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Reinforcement Learning based Traffic Signal Control for Queue Minimization: From Lane-based to Laneless Traffic
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Efficient traffic signal control (TSC) is essential for reducing congestion and delays. Traditional TSC methods struggle to capture the dynamics of laneless, heterogeneous traffic. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) based adaptive TSC framework whose reward depends only on approach-level queue length, motivated by the difficulty of obtaining per-vehicle measurements in laneless traffic, and evaluate it using SUMO on a conventional lane-based, homogeneous (LBHO) intersection and on a non-orthogonal laneless, heterogeneous (LLHE) intersection. On the LBHO site, the lowest mean configuration has about 23\% lower mean queue length than a Dynamic Webster baseline, and the unselected Full-State configuration about 15\% lower. On the LLHE site, all RL configurations have 66-73\% lower mean queue length than a Dynamic Webster baseline under nominal demand, and 63--74\% lower under two higher-demand scenarios evaluated without retraining. Our algorithm also outperforms actuated control and a RESCO-DQN baseline on mean queue length. We additionally release a laneless, heterogeneous-vehicle SUMO framework integrated with RL based signal control, to our knowledge the first such open implementation on a current SUMO version.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Attack-Aware Intrusion Risk Monitoring for Aerial Surveillance via Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper considers online intrusion-risk assessment and graded warning for unmanned aerial vehicles under bounded measurement attacks. To address this problem, we develop a monitoring framework that combines trusted state estimation, attack-aware risk assessment, and probabilistic signal temporal logic (PrSTL). Trusted observations support recursive state estimation, while potentially attacked observations inform integrity testing and intrusion-risk assessment. The key contribution is a confidence-set construction that combines normalized innovation statistics with physical attack bounds to characterize admissible measurement biases. The resulting family of bias-corrected Gaussian posteriors yields an upper bound on the probability of occupying a no-fly zone or its surrounding safety margin. Confidence guarantees and finite-cover numerical certificates quantify the reliability of this risk envelope, which is evaluated with or without an integrity alarm. The PrSTL monitor analyzes the resulting risk sequence to distinguish ordered, persistent, and repeated risk and produces graded warnings with explicit robustness margins and supporting windows. We validate the monitor in flight experiments with a Crazyflie quadrotor tracked by a Vicon motion capture system. Controlled comparisons quantify the contributions of individual monitoring components. Prescribed risk profiles verify the temporal semantics and illustrate how distinct risk patterns produce different warning levels.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Reliability-based lifetime fatigue damage assessment of offshore composite wind turbine blades
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents a method for stochastic deterioration modelling and fatigue damage assessment for composite wind turbine blades operating in offshore environments. The fatigue damage of the composite blades is analysed and assessed based on the estimates for the applied loads along the blade span, stress analysis, fatigue crack evolution, and lifetime probability of fatigue failure. The complex stress states of the blade are mainly caused by the aerodynamic loads generated by corrected blade element momentum theory, gravity loads and centrifugal loads. The fatigue of the wind turbine blade is then investigated on the basis of the actual fatigue damage propagation process. The stochastic gamma process is introduced to calculate the probability of fatigue failure of the blade for various critical limits, and these results together with lifecycle cost analysis are employed to determine the optimum maintenance strategy. Finally, a numerical example for an NREL 5 MW wind turbine blade is adopted to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method. The numerical results show that the proposed approach can provide a reliable tool for estimating stress states, evaluating fatigue damage, analysing lifetime fatigue failure probability and optimising repair time of the composite wind turbine blade.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Grasping and Stabilizing Tumbling Objects with Rotating-Base Multi-Arm Space Manipulators
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents an innovative guidance and control method for a space manipulator that actively maneuvers its base to hold a tumbling object stationary relative to the base during proximity operations. This simplifies motion planning, reduces collision risk, and enables impact-free capture using single- or multi-arm configurations, with or without predefined grasping interfaces. The proposed approach involves two phases. In the pre-grasping phase, a synchronization control aligns the target's center of mass (CoM) with the system's instantaneous center of rotation (ICR), virtually rigidizing the target-servicer system to keep the object stationary for reliable grasping. In the post grasping phase, a control strategy based on Hamiltonian dynamics and optimal control stabilizes the combined system by minimizing time, fuel, or energy, while respecting base torque limits and multiple grasping constraints. For structured targets, applied forces and torques stay within their bounds; for unstructured ones, friction constraints prevent slipping. A case study demonstrates the method's effectiveness in enabling both the subsequent grasping and detumbling phases.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Transferring Controller from Math to Real World Systems: A Formal Control Theoretic Approach
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The letter aims to improve the math-to-real or math-to-sim transfer of a mission controller designed for a Temporal Reach Avoid Stay (T-RAS) specification. Our approach uses the control-theoretic concept of Incremental Input-to-State stability ($δ$-ISS). We model the real-world system as an uncertain system, represented by a nominal mathematical model with an additive disturbance. Our method involves two steps: firstly, we make the nominal mathematical model and the real-world system $δ$-ISS. Secondly, we design a mission controller for the mathematical model that satisfies a modified specification. We then prove that applying the same mission-level input sequence to the real-world system guarantees that the original specification is satisfied in the real world. Videos of real-world experiments are available at https://youtu.be/NvjkIZxtnPM.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Translate, then decide: asymptotic optimality of latent-space control in bistable systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper asks whether an optimal decision can be separated from the physical dynamics on which it acts. It studies this question through minimum-energy barrier crossing in scalar bistable systems. It characterizes the finite-horizon optimal feedback and shows that, as the horizon grows, it converges to a law that doubles and reverses the drift while it opposes crossing, and switches off once the barrier is passed. In physical coordinates, this law inherits the plant's nonlinearity, entangling decision and dynamics. We show that a plant-specific translation of state, input, and time maps every double well in the considered class to the same unit-rate linear world model, allowing a downstream decision stage to use a single plant-independent control primitive. This separation generally loses optimality at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve the physical control energy. Nevertheless, we prove that the excess physical energy of the layered controller vanishes as the horizon grows and that its limiting feedback reproduces the asymptotic optimum exactly. Thus, translation and optimization generally do not commute at a finite horizon, but commute in the asymptotic limit.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Game-Theoretic Decision Framework for Optimal Selection of Coordination Detection Methods in Multi-UAV Fleet Operations
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Detecting coordination among unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) fleets operating in shared airspace and identifying the route-lead aircraft whose navigation decisions govern fleet behavior presents a fundamental speed--accuracy trade-off: fast methods enable real-time traffic management but sacrifice detection fidelity, while accurate methods may exceed the time budget for actionable airspace deconfliction. This paper presents a game-theoretic decision framework that resolves this trade-off by formulating method selection as a two-player zero-sum game between a Monitor (selecting computational methods and parameters) and Nature (selecting the unknown traffic scenario). We construct an end-to-end pipeline from trajectory surveillance data through eight candidate detection algorithms, a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis characterizing their stochastic performance, and finally a multi-objective optimization layer that identifies Pareto-optimal method portfolios. The minimax solution provides a robust mixed strategy with a probability distribution over methods that guarantees worst-case performance regardless of scenario uncertainty. Experimental evaluation across 200 randomized configurations spanning 5--50 aircraft demonstrates that the framework recommends distinct method portfolios depending on operational priority: Koopman Phase dominates balanced (70.6%) and speed-priority (79.7%) profiles, while CRQA emerges as primary (47.4%) when route-lead identification is prioritized. The framework achieves a guaranteed game value of 0.29--0.53 (normalized utility) across all tested preference profiles, providing the first principled, scenario-adaptive methodology for computational method selection in UTM fleet monitoring operations.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Decentralized Impedance Specifications for Grid-Connected Converters: a Sequence-Domain Gershgorin Method, and a Frequency-Wise Framework for Combining Different Criteria
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In complex grid scenarios, with many power electronics (PE) converters connected, having specifications for converters can ease the design process. A practical approach is to impose the specifications on the converter's small-signal impedance in the frequency domain. This is advantageous since impedance is a physical property that can be measured. This paper focuses on providing decentralized impedance specifications for each converter connected to an ac bus. With decentralized specifications, each converter has its own specifications, which are independent of other converters' impedance. This enables a competitive multi-vendor environment while guaranteeing system stability. Existing methods of imposing decentralized specifications, based on the small-gain, passivity and Gershgorin theorems, are formulated within a common frequency-domain framework. Building on this, two new solutions that reduce the conservativeness of the specifications are proposed. First, Gershgorin-based decentralized specifications are formulated in the modified sequence domain. Second, a framework for combining different specification types across frequency ranges is developed and mathematically proven. The methods are compared on examples covering sub-synchronous and harmonic-range interactions of grid-following converters, grid-forming converters, and a mixed grid-forming/grid-following system, using analytical models, black-box impedance measurements, and time-domain responses obtained from simulations and an experimental setup.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Model Predictive Control of Heating Systems via Koopman-Operator Bilinearization
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Hydronic heat emitters are widely used in buildings, but their control is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics, arising from both the heat transfer in each emitter and the hydraulic coupling among those that share a circulating pump. These nonlinearities are often simplified or neglected in the literature. In this paper, we use Koopman theory to make the resulting model more tractable for control. In particular, we propose an input reparameterization and construct an infinite-dimensional set of observables that yields an exact bilinear representation of the system in the chosen lifted space. We then show that truncating the infinite-dimensional representation leads to bounded approximation errors that decrease as the truncation order increases, as well as bounded trajectory deviations over a finite horizon. The resulting bilinear model is incorporated into a model predictive control (MPC) framework to provide thermal comfort in multi-zone buildings while reducing energy use. Using a numerical case study of a five-story building with 20 zones, we show that the proposed Koopman-based MPC achieves a realized performance cost close to that of nonlinear MPC with faster solve times, and outperforms MPC formulations based on time-invariant and time-varying linearizations.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Barrier-State-Based Safe Navigation in Complex Environments Using Look-Ahead Safety Corridors
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Safe navigation in cluttered environments requires a safety representation that captures the available motion space along the planned path. A single local safe region may restrict progress through narrow passages and continuous turns. This paper presents a planning-guided look-ahead safety corridor framework for barrier-state-based navigation. Local safe convex polytopes are constructed around collision-free seeds along the forward reference path. Their facet constraints are combined using softmin, and the local functions are fused using softmax with entropy-based adaptive compensation. The resulting safe set remains within the union of the local polytopes while reducing the shrinkage caused by fixed compensation. A Poisson boundary-value problem then defines a differentiable interior safety field while preserving the prescribed corridor boundary. This field is embedded into the robot dynamics through one geometric barrier state.
