Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Autonomous precision milling of biological structures is challenged by incomplete knowledge of target geometry, local material thickness, and critical internal boundaries. Subject-specific preoperative models can address geometric and thickness variations, but static models cannot determine boundary status encountered during execution, while repeated target-specific imaging limits scalability. This article presents a state-adaptive autonomous milling framework that assigns complementary roles to generic anatomical priors and active boundary perception. A generic anatomical prior provides conservative global guidance and is transformed through semantic-guided registration and hybrid vision-force calibration into robot-executable guidance for individual targets. As milling approaches uncertain boundaries, the robot actively probes the remaining structure and uses relative stiffness changes to estimate boundary status and structural detachability. A state-adaptive controller governs transitions between active perception and spatially selective incremental refinement, repeating this cycle until the termination criterion is satisfied. Hierarchical experiments on biological surrogates and in vivo mouse cranial window creation demonstrate accurate anatomical prior transfer, reliable boundary adaptation, and autonomous precision milling of biological structures.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: ver 2. 18 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering (T-ASE) for possible publication

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Degradation-Aware Participation of Battery Storage in Frequency Regulation Markets
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: As data centers make the load on the power grid fluctuate faster, frequency regulation grows more valuable. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) are well suited to provide frequency regulation, but providing this service speeds up aging, especially during operation at extreme state of charge (SoC). In the PJM interconnection, the grid operator supplies a regulation signal that a participating BESS is expected to follow, within a capacity that it must bid before the signal is known. Accordingly, we decompose the degradation-aware frequency regulation problem into a bidding layer and an operations layer. For bidding, we propose an adaptive strategy, assuming perfect tracking in which the bid depends on the SoC expected at the start of the bid period by means of choosing basepoints. For operation, the BESS further protects its battery by deliberately giving up a perfect performance score, to keep its SoC away from the extremes. On the PJM regulation signal and prices of 2023, adaptive bids lengthen the battery life by $31\%$ against bidding full capacity, for $2.2\%$ of the revenue. Giving up a perfect score in operation lengthens the battery life of constant bids by $10\%$ to $27\%$, at a change in revenue of at most $0.2\%$.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Extended version of IEEE PESGM submission

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Characterization of the Frequency-Current Curve of First-Order High-Pass Neurons
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: A spiking model, called the High-Pass (HP) model, has recently been proposed as a minimal excitable primitive. This model is composed of a static activation function, usually a sigmoid, in positive feedback with a high-pass filter. The HP model enters a tonic spiking regime whenever its input lies in the high-gain zone of the sigmoid, where the sigmoid's slope exceeds 1. In neuroscience, the frequency-current (FI) curve is the standard way of characterizing the tonic spiking regime of a neuron. So far, the FI curve of the HP model has been characterized analytically only for specific sigmoids, and has otherwise been computed through simulation. These simulations are computationally heavy, since simulating neurons requires solving a stiff system of differential equations. This paper bridges this gap by analytically characterizing the FI curve of the HP model with a first-order high-pass filter, for a broad class of sigmoid functions. The FI curve of the first-order HP model can be computed by solving two input-independent equations and evaluating two input-dependent integrals, with no need to simulate the model itself. A spiking primitive is said to be Type I (resp. Type II) if tonic spiking starts at a zero (resp. non-zero) frequency. This paper also shows that, for the HP model, the type depends solely on the local shape of the sigmoid at the outer edges of its high-gain zone. A sharp corner, where the derivative approaches a value strictly smaller than 1 from the outside, yields a Type I primitive. A locally twice differentiable corner, with a bounded second derivative and a derivative approaching 1 at the edge, yields a Type II primitive.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Towards Passivity-informed Data-driven Predictive Control
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We propose a passivity-informed data-driven predictive control framework based on passivity-preserving sampling of unknown continuous-time linear systems. We incorporate the passive supply rate into the objective functional alongside an output-regulation cost, thereby explicitly accounting for energy extraction. Despite being practically motivated, the resulting objective is not always convex; its convexity depends on the collected input-output training data. We exploit passivity-induced positive semidefiniteness to derive an equivalent reformulation that remains a convex quadratic program independently of the data. Furthermore, we establish recursive feasibility and asymptotic output convergence using passivity and a terminal equality constraint. Numerical simulations illustrate the closed-loop performance and computational benefits of the proposed approach.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Towards Optimal Passive Feedback Control of LTI Systems under LQR Performance
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study state-feedback design for continuous-time LTI systems with a control input and an external input-output pair. Our objective is to determine feedback gains that render the closed-loop system (strictly) passive with respect to the external port while minimizing the standard LQR cost in the disturbance-free case. The resulting constrained optimization problem is intractable due to bilinear matrix inequalities. We analyze the set of passivating gains, showing it is unbounded, possibly nonconvex, path-connected, and contractible. We propose an indirect approach, in which the set of passivating feedback gains is inner-approximated by a compact, convex polytope. A projected gradient flow is employed to compute a gain within this polytope that minimizes the LQR cost. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of the method.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Design and Formulation of a Hydromechanical Fin for AUV Operations and Wave Parameter Estimation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Ocean dynamics play a crucial role in global climate, ecosystems, and human activities, necessitating accurate and efficient methods to characterize ocean currents and waves. This paper presents the development of a novel bio-inspired hydrofoil system for detecting and characterizing ocean currents and waves based on a dolphin's flipper foil design. The prototype's performance was assessed through controlled experiments, demonstrating the system's ability to quickly and accurately orientate itself in the direction of flow. Wave mechanics and a geometric proof were applied to estimate wave parameters such as wave height and current from the hydrofoil's positioning. The proposed hydrofoil system shows potential for use in various marine applications, including oceanographic research, environmental monitoring, and navigation. The bio-inspired hydrofoil system offers a promising approach to ocean current and wave characterization, with the potential to significantly impact our understanding and monitoring of ocean dynamics without greatly impacting vehicle performance or increasing power utilization in operation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: KPG193-ext: A Synthetic Korean Power Grid Test System for Stability Analysis
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Growing shares of inverter-based generation and constrained transmission expansion increase the need to assess stability across operating conditions. Production-cost models provide chronological commitment and dispatch, but stability analysis requires corresponding electrical detail and device dynamics. This paper introduces KPG193-ext, an extension of the synthetic Korean power-grid test system KPG193 that links chronological operating points with detailed electrical and dynamic models. The extension adds synchronous-machine, controller and renewable-converter models, together with explicit voltage levels, generation terminals, inter-voltage and step-up transformers, and reactive compensation. The resulting 731-bus network retains the original 193 regional locations. Daily unit commitment followed by hourly AC optimal power flow establishes 8,760 operating points for 2025, each distributed as paired steady-state and dynamic-model files. Selected-hour studies examine generation-loss frequency response, steady-state flow-voltage characteristics, and rotor-angle response with special protection system actions. The results reveal differences in delivered frequency support, internal voltage stress along regional transfer paths, and the angle-frequency tradeoff of corrective generator tripping. The database provides a common basis for examining the stability implications of commitment, dispatch and corrective action across daily and seasonal operating conditions.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Scalable Practical Synchronization of Heterogeneous Linear Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study practical state synchronization of heterogeneous linear multi-agent systems over directed graphs using static diffusive state feedback. Persistent mismatches between the agent dynamics generally preclude exact synchronization and are treated as bounded disturbances within an Input-to-State Stability (ISS) framework. We derive a scalable synthesis procedure based on fixed-dimension linear matrix inequalities (LMIs), whose dimension is independent of the number of agents. Local robust dissipation conditions are combined through a small-gain argument to obtain global ISS guarantees and explicit bounds on the synchronization error. The framework is formulated in a unified manner for continuous- and discrete-time systems, while highlighting a fundamental difference in disturbance attenuation between the two domains. In particular, exact ZOH discretization of a continuous-time controller need not preserve closed-loop stability, motivating a native discrete-time synthesis. Numerical experiments on heterogeneous harmonic oscillators illustrate the proposed approach and the continuous/discrete-time distinction.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Sensor placement for real-life water distribution networks, ensuring observability under uncertainties
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Leakage detection in water distribution networks (WDNs) is crucial for limiting water losses. However, effective detection strongly depends on sensor availability and placement. Most existing sensor placement methods rely on extensive simulations or precise knowledge of hydraulic parameters, which are often uncertain in practice. In this paper, we propose using a scalable sensor placement framework based on structural observability that depends only on the network topology and the underlying pressure-flow interconnection structure. The approach guarantees structural observability independently of hydraulic parameters, and is therefore robust to parametric uncertainties, assuming that the network topology is correctly specified. The method is computationally efficient and its performance is demonstrated on several real-life WDNs provided by Brabant-Water. While the framework ensures full network observability, the required number of sensors can be high in large and cyclic networks, which may limit applicability in real-life and motivates future work on relaxed observability guarantees for sensor placement.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Observer-based parameter estimation in a Darcy model towards dam internal seepage monitoring with validation on real data
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper addresses internal seepage monitoring in hydraulic infrastructures through the estimation of physical parameters in a distributed model. A physics-based approach relying on Darcy's law is adopted to describe the spatiotemporal evolution of hydraulic head within the structure. To enable real-time applicability, a Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to derive a reduced-order model of the underlying partial differential equation. An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is then designed to perform online estimation of the hydraulic diffusivity, a key parameter related to the structural state. The proposed method is validated directly on real measurement data through a twofold approach. First, the estimated parameter is compared with the value obtained via offline batch optimization performed on the same dataset, showing consistent results. Second, the ability of the resulting model, parametrized by the estimated diffusivity, to reconstruct the observed measurements is assessed, to evaluate its suitability for seepage monitoring.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Safety-Constrained Intelligent Control of a 2-DOF Robotic Manipulator Using Control Barrier Functions
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Paper submitted to the European Control Conference 2027

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Tutorial on Learning-Based Radio Map Construction: Data, Paradigms, and Physics-Awareness
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Radio maps (RMs) provide the digital representation of the wireless propagation environment, mapping complex geographical and topological boundary conditions to critical spatial-spectral metrics that range from received signal strength to full channel state information matrices. The integration of artificial intelligence into next generation wireless networks further necessitates the accurate construction of RMs as a foundational prerequisite for electromagnetic digital twins. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of learning-based RM construction, systematically addressing three intertwined dimensions: data, paradigms, and physics-awareness. From the data perspective, we review physical measurement campaigns, ray tracing simulation engines, and publicly available benchmark datasets, identifying their respective strengths and fundamental limitations. From the paradigm perspective, we establish a core taxonomy that categorizes RM construction into source-aware forward prediction and \added{source-agnostic} inverse reconstruction, and examine five principal neural architecture families spanning convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, graph neural networks, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models. We further survey optics-inspired methods adapted from neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting for continuous wireless radiation field modeling. From the physics-awareness perspective, we introduce a three-level integration framework encompassing data-level feature engineering, loss-level partial differential equation regularization, and \added{architecture-level} structural isomorphism. Open challenges including foundation model development, physical hallucination detection, and amortized inference for real-time deployment are discussed to outline future research directions.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Tensor Network Kernel Machines for Nonlinear System Identification
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Over the past ten years Tensor Network Kernel Machines have enabled efficient nonlinear system identification through the use of low-rank tensor networks. The goal of this article is to provide the reader with a basic understanding of this model class in terms of its two defining properties. Furthermore, both the optimization and regularization of such models are discussed, together with recent developments and starting points for further exploration.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: This work has been submitted to IFAC for possible publication

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Scale-Space Theory of Memory
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Scale-space theory has emerged as a central attempt to restrict the {\it general} theory of signal processing with geometric constraints inspired from the animal world. In the mathematical language of operator theory, scale-space theory restricts the Toeplitz operator. The present paper investigates scale-space theory for memory systems. We investigate how scale space theory restricts a memory system encoding past information, that is, restricts the Hankel operator. Our main result is to establish a close correspondence between scale-space theory and the long-studied {\it relaxation} property.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Price-Optimized EV and Heat-Pump Scheduling Can Exceed Uncoordinated Feeder Peaks
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Electric vehicles and heat pumps add large, time-flexible loads to low-voltage feeders. When each household independently minimizes its own charging cost against the same electricity price, this flexible demand piles into the cheapest hours, and the resulting synchronization can stress the feeder more than uncoordinated operation does. This work quantifies that effect on a rural low-voltage feeder with photovoltaics (97 buses, 250 kVA transformer) in 913 simulation runs that compare seven strategies across four seasons, device penetrations of up to 90 %, 208 price weeks from 2022-2025, and heterogeneous heat pumps. At 30 % penetration of each device, this decentralized cost minimization drives the transformer to 253 % of rated capacity, more than three times the peak of non-optimized Fixed-random charging with the same mobility and charged energy, and 478 % with electric vehicles alone at 90 % penetration, with undervoltage at the far end of the longest feeder arm. It exceeds Fixed-random and Fixed-times charging in every winter, spring, and autumn price week, and each 30 pp of heat-pump penetration raises its peak by about 110 pp, twelve times as much as without optimization. Centralized peak minimization removes all demand-driven violations. In the heat-pump-free summer case at 60 % photovoltaics, midday reverse power flow sets a transformer floor of 128.9 % that no strategy undercuts, since no commuting electric vehicle is at home at the export peak. With a time-variable grid fee added to the spot price, the weekly peak of decentralized cost minimization falls into the reduced-fee window in 99 of the 104 fee-active price weeks, compared with 53 without the fee, while keeping at least 89.8 % of its height, so the fee relocates rather than removes the synchronization. The simulation and optimization code is available at https://github.com/lukas-wagner/SynchronizationEffectsAnalysis.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Prospective Action-Resource Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Electric HGV Fleets under Shared Charging Infrastructure
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Electric heavy goods vehicle (eHGV) fleet coordination requires each vehicle to choose driving, charging and resting actions whose consequences depend on shared infrastructure. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods mainly represent current states, leaving action-specific futures and resource interactions to be learned indirectly. We develop Horizon-Preview and Graph-Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimisation (HGC-PPO), which integrates horizon preview and candidate-resource graph coordination into the PPO decision architecture. Horizon preview represents each legal action through its short-horizon operational consequences. Graph message passing then updates these candidates through station, charger-type and time-slot resources shared across the fleet. On the 794km Folkestone-Glasgow task, HGC-PPO achieved the lowest mean charging cost among five RL methods at £504.32 per vehicle, with a fleet completion time of 24.920h. It also completed the task 1.763h faster and cost £36.51 less per vehicle than a replay-verified finite-budget MILP benchmark. Across six unseen routes and fleet sizes from 5 to 20 vehicles, HGC-PPO delivered the lowest macro-average completion time, charging cost and charging frequency among the RL methods. A 2 by 2 ablation showed that the full preview-graph architecture performed best across all four operational metrics. These results show that prospective action information and fleet-wide resource coordination improve eHGV decisions under charging and driver-hours constraints.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Game-Theoretic MPC Planner for Cooperative and Adversarial Drone Coordination
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, submitted to European Control Conference (ECC27)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Environmental Assessment of GaN Current-Source and Voltage-Source AC-AC Variable Speed Drives
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Three-phase ac-ac converters for variable-speed drives can be realized conventionally as voltage-source converters (VSCs) or, leveraging emerging monolithic bidirectional GaN power transistors (M-BDSs), as current-source converters (CSCs). This paper presents a comparative life-cycle assessment of a realized VSC and a CSC demonstrators including grid-side and motor-side EMI filters, and with identical specifications (1.4 kW rated power, 200 V line-to-line rms grid and motor voltage). The embodied carbon footprints are similar (44.8 kgCO2eq for the VSC and 47.4 kgCO2eq for the CSC) and dominated by auxiliary and control electronics, and the printed circuit boards. Over 10 years of continuous operation under the NEMA Power Index mission profile for variable-load centrifugal systems (pumps, fans), the CSC's higher part-load efficiency translates into a clearly lower life-cycle carbon footprint of around 900 kgCO2eq compared to the VSC's 1130 kgCO2eq when operating with a carbon-intense electricity mix (440 gCO2eq/kWh). However, this difference almost vanishes when considering a future renewable electricity mix (25 gCO2eq/kWh).

Systems and Control (EESS).title: DC Voltage Control Dominated Oscillations in Electromechanical Frequency Range - Insights from Synchronous Coefficient Reduction Effect of IBR Plants and Network Interactions
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Large-scale integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is widely known to cause subsynchronous oscillations. This paper investigates a distinct class of oscillations that occur in the electromechanical frequency range (EFR), referred to as EFOs, and are dominated by the DC voltage control (DVC) loops of grid-following IBRs rather than synchronous generator-like controls or phase-locked loops (PLLs). Although open-loop oscillation modes of DVC loops are subsynchronous, the corresponding closed-loop dominant oscillation mode related to DVC can shift downward into the EFR without retuning the control parameters. This frequency shift is caused by network-mediated interactions among the IBRs, which introduce a negative synchronous coefficient into the DVC oscillation loop. This synchronous coefficient reduction effect (SCRE) becomes stronger as the IBR plant scale increases and/or as the minimum eigenvalue of the network admittance matrix decreases. Furthermore, a complex vector-based stability analysis method is proposed, and a stability criterion for DVC-EFOs is derived. Finally, the analytical conclusions are validated using a practical power system configuration implemented in Simulink. The SCRE differs from traditional explanations, in which the open-loop oscillation modes are already located in the EFR, and provides new insight into DVC-dominated oscillations in the EFR for integration of IBR plants.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: On necessary conditions for feedback stabilizability when the control space is a fiber bundle
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Within control theory, a question of great interest is to understand when a stabilizing feedback exists. Building upon Krasnosel'skiĭ and co-workers, necessary conditions for the existence of a continuous stabilizing feedback have been pioneered by Brockett and Coron, providing so-called adversarial and homological conditions, respectively. Kvalheim recently generalized their conditions from equilibria to compact attractors and---in line with earlier work by Coron---showed that when a control system can be identified with a vector bundle, the homology condition is stronger, that is, the homology condition implies the adversary condition. Kvalheim also showed that this comparison breaks when extending the case of vector bundles to fiber bundles. In this work, we propose and characterize an appropriate adversarial condition for control systems represented by fiber bundles. The homology condition, on the other hand, is already well-defined, showcasing its general applicability. With the generalized conditions at hand, we show that by appropriately relaxing the regularity of the feedback under consideration, that is, by allowing for mild discontinuities, the homology condition implies the adversarial condition for fiber bundles. Thereby, in this work, we extend these earlier comparative results.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Compact and Wide-Force-Range Magnetorheological Hand Exoskeleton for Kinesthetic Feedback in Teleoperation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Hand kinesthetic feedback is crucial for restoring and enhancing human perception of force and displacement in robotic hand teleoperation. Wide perception range of force feedback is vital in rendering objects of different stiffness, especially for high-stiffness rendering. However, existing approaches struggle to achieve wide range of force feedback while maintaining compact and wearable design. This paper presents a hand exoskeleton system employing magnetorheological (MR) brakes to provide a wide range kinesthetic feedback during teleoperation. The MR brake provides a braking torque ranging from 0.01 to 0.918 Nm, while maintaining a compact structure with a total mass of only 39.8 g. The proposed exoskeleton can render fingertip forces up to 21 N while maintaining back-driving force of 1.01 N. Experimental results show that the system allows users to discriminate object stiffness using kinesthetic feedback alone. In a tele-grasping task, when both conditions achieved a 100% success rate, kinesthetic feedback led to a 28.2% reduction in object contact force compared to visual feedback only, enhancing object safety and operator immersion. Questionnaire results further indicate that kinesthetic feedback improves reliability, realism, and user confidence during teleoperation.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: First-order plants are globally asymptotically stable under antithetic feedback
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We show that first-order linear plants are globally asymptotically stable under antithetic feedback. This is shown by constructing an explicit smooth, convex Lyapunov function and by appealing to a Krasovskii-LaSalle invariance principle.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Repeated Binary Direct Collinear Impacts Under Incremental Contact Laws With Residual Indentation: A Hybrid Systems Formulation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Incremental contact laws specify the normal contact force through a differential relation, possibly carrying an internal state, driven by the indentation and its rate. The force may vanish at a nonzero indentation, through plasticity, an elastic aftereffect, or, under some laws with a viscous component, a load drawing the bodies apart rapidly, leaving a residual deformation at separation. Such a deformation sits uneasily within rigid body dynamics, which admits none. The tension is tolerable when the indentation is small relative to the bodies, so that it may be carried constitutively rather than geometrically. Even then, the law alone does not determine the interaction: because force and indentation no longer vanish together, conditions for the commencement and termination of contact must be supplied separately, as must the fate of the deformation and internal state at separation, both absent from the equations of motion. This article formulates the repeated direct collinear impact of two convex bodies under external forces as a hybrid dynamical system. The contact interface is modeled as a massless element carrying the contact law and its state, coupled to the bodies through relative velocity and an interaction force dictated by the contact state. Consequently, all switching and resets are confined to the interface, leaving the geometry and equations of motion of the bodies unaltered. The principal analytical properties of the formulations are established, among them passivity and completeness; the branching of solutions at the onset and termination of contact is examined. The framework is demonstrated through numerical simulations.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 34 pages, 6 figures; v1-v7: a variety of amendments and corrections; v6-v7: further analytical properties

Systems and Control (EESS).title: One number per hour is not enough: directional carbon intensity of data-center ramps on the PJM fleet
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: A data-center campus can change its load by hundreds of megawatts within an hour, yet every carbon signal in use gives one value per hour for a load change, whatever its size or direction. We compute the directional carbon intensity, the emission caused or avoided per megawatt-hour of a finite upward or downward ramp, for every hour of 2025 on the PJM Interconnection's fossil fleet, and compare it with the locational marginal emission rate (LME) and the regional average. The LME misstates a 1 GW ramp by more than 10% in 60% to 83% of hours in eleven months. Upward and downward ramps differ in a quarter to three quarters of hours but agree on their monthly mean. Location-based reporting assigns 47% to 59% of a ramp's emission to other consumers. A campus should schedule on the signal for its ramp's size and direction and report the emission it causes.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 15 pages main text, 6 pages supplemental information. Code and derived results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24074188

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Update-v2: add stepwise falsification guarantee theorem, VLA experiments, and acknowledgment

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Online Digital Twins: Data Assimilation and Control
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The online assimilation of data and the application of controls are essential ingredients of the digital twin paradigm. In this paper, we formalize the online interaction between the physical process and its virtual digital representation in the setting of continuously arriving data from the physical process and a receding horizon virtual planning process, which provides the control for the physical process. Our mathematical formulation relies on a mean field representation of the data assimilation process as well as a mean field Pontryagin minimum principle for the optimal control problem. Such mean field formulations are computationally attractive because they allow for simultaneous implementation in terms of Hamiltonian interacting particle systems. A more detailed discussion is included for the ensemble Kalman-Bucy filter in combination with affine approximations of the receding horizon control laws. This paper sets out the mathematical framework, while a computational study is left for future research.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Generalizable Output Feedback Optimal Control via Transformers Without Explicit State Estimation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Classical optimal control is used to design a separate controller for each plant. This paper asks a different question. Can one learned policy serve a whole family of partially observed, noisy linear systems? We show that one transformer can. The policy is trained to imitate optimal LQG control on a heterogeneous family of Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems with Multiple Inputs and Multiple Outputs (MIMO), whose dimensions, cost matrices, and noise levels all vary. A shared representation with system-wise standardization, zero-padding, masking, and an encoding of the cost and noise covariances lets one set of weights control every member of the family. At run time, a short window of noisy measurements is all the policy needs to produce a control action, with no plant matrices and no state estimator. We characterize the relation between the optimal LQG policy (represented as a dynamic state-space model) and a static transformer acting on a finite window of measurements. We then express the closed-loop excess cost of any causal policy as the energy of its deviation from the optimal action. Finally, we evaluate the approach on 28 simulated systems. The trained policy reaches the optimal cost to within a median gap of $0.4\%$ for seen systems. For unseen systems, a light fine-tuning step brings the median gap to $1.0\%$.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: MAC+: Mobility-Aware Co-Expansion Planning for Distribution Grid and Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study the least-cost co-expansion of power distribution networks and public charging ports to accommodate the growth of electric vehicles (EVs). Our approach, MAC+, exploits the flexibility of charging along each EV's itinerary and coordinates it across the fleet to reduce the peak violations of each feeder's hosting capacity and port capacity. This coordination is an extremely large, spatio-temporally coupled optimization problem with binary plug-in variables. We solve it by iterated price response (IPR), which repeatedly posts a two-tier tariff on feeder load and port occupancy, lets millions of EVs best-respond in parallel, and certifies the optimality gap at every iteration. We develop a custom exact dynamic-programming algorithm that solves each EV's best-response problem, a mixed-integer quadratic program, about 20 times faster than off-the-shelf solvers. The case study covers the San Francisco Bay Area at 30% EV adoption, with 1.8 million EVs on week-long itineraries and 1,303 feeder service regions, each with a utility-published hosting capacity and a port capacity set by its existing public ports. On this instance, IPR reaches a certified gap below 10% in a few hours. MAC+ saves about $15 billion of the upgrade investment that unmanaged charging would require. It also needs over 90% less investment than charging that is fully coordinated but flexible only within each session, and over 80% less than charging that is flexible along the itinerary but uncoordinated.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Graph-Sparse Distributed Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning vianEdge-Consensus ADMM
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper presents a distributed model predictive control (MPC) architecture for collision-avoiding motion planning of planar robots with double-integrator dynamics. To reduce coordination demands, a time-varying predicted conflict graph selects relevant pairwise interactions. The associated collision-avoidance constraints are convexified once per MPC update using warm-start trajectories, yielding a fixed convex quadratic program (QP). The resulting QP is then decomposed using an edge-consensus formulation of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), enabling parallel robot-local optimization and independent closed-form projections onto separating half-spaces. Execution is selectively supervised by a centralized high-order control barrier function (HOCBF) QP when the distributed candidate does not satisfy the direct-execution conditions. Evaluated in C++ simulations involving 8, 16, and 32 robots, the proposed architecture achieves collision-free execution and substantially improves computational scalability while maintaining task-level performance comparable to a centralized complete-graph baseline.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Bifurcation-Theoretic Framework for the Controllability of Emergent Intelligent Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Real-world intelligent systems must reconcile two demands: the adaptability conferred by emergence and the steerability required for accountable deployment. We show that these demands are governed by two distinct bifurcations on the same object and that, consequently, increased capability does not imply increased controllability. Emergence is a bifurcation of the capability variable $S$, with criterion $Γ:=\mathcal F'(0)>1$ equivalent to the existence of a unique positive stable fixed point of a self-consistency equation, following solely from the concavity of $\mathcal F$. Controllability is a bifurcation of the permission variable $c$, whose dynamics include an erosion term and exhibit a saddle-node fold with hysteresis as the gate criterion $ρ^\ast$ crosses unity. Three quantitative results follow: the critical exponent distinguishes families rather than classifying the transition; the gating-cost bound $K(M)\propto\log(1+M)$ grows with scope, not capability; and the fold threshold is $γ_c\approx4μκ$. Calibrated in both directions, the criteria reproduce the two-dimensional Ising transition, admit two true-feedback order parameters, and reject nine candidate quantities, supporting the conclusion that the order parameter is geometric rather than capability-related. Since permission cannot be endogenized and no deployed system has been measured to satisfy $Γ>1$ and $ρ^\ast>1$ simultaneously, increased capability does not imply controllability.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: The Smart Buildings Control Suite: A Diverse Open Source Benchmark to Evaluate and Scale HVAC Control Policies for Sustainability
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Commercial buildings account for 17\% of U.S. carbon emissions, with roughly half of that from Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC). HVAC devices form a complex thermodynamic system, and while model predictive control and reinforcement learning have been used to optimize control policies, scaling to thousands of buildings remains a significant unsolved challenge. Most current approaches are over-optimized for specific buildings and rely on proprietary data or hard-to-configure simulators. We present the Smart Buildings Control Suite, the first open source interactive HVAC control benchmark with a focus on solutions that generalize across building. It has 3 components: real-world data from 11 buildings over 6 years, a lightweight data-driven simulator, and a modular Physically Informed Neural Network (PINN) building model. The buildings span multiple climates, management systems, and sizes, and both the simulator and PINN easily transfer to new buildings, ensuring solutions using this benchmark are robust to these factors and only reliant on fully scalable building models. This represents a major step towards scaling HVAC optimization from the lab to buildings everywhere. To facilitate use, our benchmark is compatible with the Gym standard, and our data is available at our webpage. Code at https://github.com/google/sbsim

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Scarcity Pricing for State-of-Charge Management in Real-Time Markets Under Intra-Day Uncertainty
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The growth in renewable resources will increase net load variability and forecast error. Energy storage resources can provide flexibility when ramp capability is limited and contribute to load leveling over the day. The challenge for system operators is how to balance these two functions in real time, when updated net load forecasts are available for a limited lookahead horizon. U.S. electricity markets are seeking ways to manage state-of-charge (SoC) within their energy markets to more efficiently utilize these resources. We propose a method to manage energy storage SoC in a real-time market by extending Hogan's (2013) scarcity pricing framework. A day-ahead SoC schedule is modified using existing multi-interval real-time unit commitment engines as net load forecasts change. To address 30-minute-ahead forecast errors, an updated 5-minute SoC target and a dynamically updated shortage price for violating the constraint are provided to each economic dispatch. We simulate PJM's energy markets for 365 days and demonstrate reliability improvements relative to a strategy that enforces the day-ahead schedule. We show cost reductions and improved price formation relative to a strategy that updates target quantities but uses an administratively chosen shortage penalty.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Passive Identification of Unequal Phase Grid Impedances by Phase-Domain Source Cancellation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Passive grid impedance estimators that return a single resistance--inductance pair cannot represent a grid whose phase impedances are unequal. This paper identifies a separate pair for each phase from recorded point-of-common-coupling (PCC) voltage and current without injected perturbations. In each phase, the unknown grid-source voltage is cancelled by a periodic difference (PD) or by a second-order-generalized-integrator notch difference (SOGID), and moving-window integration (MWI) replaces the current derivative by an integral and an endpoint feature. The resulting two-parameter regression requires a period or notch-frequency estimate but no phase-locked-loop angle. A voltage-balance analysis gives the source residual left by frequency mismatch and bounds the parameter error by the ratio of this residual to the conditioning of the two features. In the unequal-phase interval (8.3--9.8~s) of a 10-s EMTP grid-forming record, SOGID-MWI attains phase-averaged R/L errors of 5.09/0.33\%; a shared value has a minimum error of 41.67\% for the phase ratio 1:0.5:2. On a 50-s constant-impedance grid-following record, the errors are 0.56/0.06\% over the 20--30-s synchronization disturbance. In a controlled 40-dB noise study, a noise-referenced update rule reduces the white-noise GFL error from 55.9/65.0\% to 12.3/11.5\%.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Rapid Heat Removal from Chip Cores: Near-Junction Active Cooling of Power Transistors via Electron Entropy Transport and Spatial Decoupling
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Chip performance is limited by a shared bottleneck: the core produces heat faster than it can be moved out. We study the hardest case, RF power GaN HEMTs, whose hotspots exceed 5 kW/cm^2, and propose a horizontal near-junction active cooling topology built on electron entropy transport. Classical on-chip thermoelectric cooling faces a contest: Peltier absorption grows linearly with current, Joule heating with its square. In a vertical pillar, its own conduction resistance locks about half the Joule heat back toward the cold end, capping net cooling. From the Onsager framework we show the origin of this asymmetry: Peltier absorption localizes at the interface where the Seebeck coefficient jumps, whereas Joule heating fills the volume. The topology exploits this: a thermoelectric thin film lies flat on a diamond substrate beside the device drain (the electron exit), so bulk Joule heat leaves vertically into the substrate. A lateral fin model gives a closed form for the recirculation factor gamma: the vertical pillar yields gamma = 1, while the horizontal film yields gamma_max = sqrt(2) L_z/L_x, about 0.03 for L_z = 10 um, L_x = 500 um. The decoupling scales the net cooling ceiling and the critical runaway current by roughly 1/gamma. At equal resistance, the same film lifts maximum cooling from 13 mW to 500 mW, and the critical current from 0.65 A to 24 A. A time-constant and linear stability analysis with temperature-sensitive parameters defines the working window and safety margins for microsecond pulse cooling. The architecture leaves the device structure untouched; the principle, absorb at an interface and extract bulk heat vertically, applies to any chip with a hot core and offers a reproducible design path for near-junction thermal management.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Informed Posterior Sampling: More Efficient Online Learning with Few Offline Demonstrations in Average-Reward MDPs
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We study efficient online reinforcement learning in the infinite horizon setting when there is an offline dataset to start with. We assume that the offline dataset is generated by an expert but with an unknown level of competence, i.e., it is not perfect and not necessarily using the optimal policy. We show that if the learning agent models the behavioral policy (parameterized by a competence parameter) used by the expert, it can do substantially better in terms of minimizing cumulative regret than if it does not do that. We establish an upper bound on regret of the exact informed PSRL (iPSRL) algorithm that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$. This requires a novel prior-dependent regret analysis of Bayesian online learning algorithms for the infinite horizon setting. We then propose the informed RLSVI (iRLSVI) algorithm to efficiently approximate the iPSRL algorithm. Empirical results show that small offline expert datasets are sufficient for iRLSVI to outperform online-only algorithms on hard exploration domains.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: AHEADance: Anticipatory Humanoid Dance from Streaming Audio
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Modal-Augmented Chebyshev Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Power Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a promising alternative to numerical integration for power system dynamic simulation; however, their conventional architectures can struggle to capture electromechanical oscillations. Although physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (PIKANs) offer an alternative, their B-spline implementations incur substantial training costs. To address these limitations, this paper investigates Chebyshev PIKANs (c-PIKANs) and proposes a modal-augmented c-PIKAN (mac-PIKAN) based on a trial solution that incorporates the closed-form modal response of the linearized swing equation. First, the modal response is used to capture the dominant oscillatory dynamics. Then, a c-PIKAN learns a nonlinear correction weighted by a quadratic time-dependent factor, ensuring that the initial rotor angle and speed are satisfied exactly. Evaluations on the single-machine infinite-bus benchmark demonstrate the computational efficiency of c-PIKAN and show that mac-PIKAN reduces PINN rotor-angle and frequency errors from 1.59% to 0.29% and from 5.26% to 0.99%, respectively, while maintaining higher accuracy across training-data sizes and at lower damping levels.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting. Code and data: https://github.com/komeilnosrati/mac-PIKAN

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Spurious-Free Lithium Niobate Bulk Acoustic Wave Resonator with Grounded-Ring Electrode
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: High-performance piezoelectric resonators are promising energy-storage elements for piezoelectric power conversion because of their compact footprint and low loss at frequencies where conventional magnetic components become bulky and inefficient. However, their practical use is often limited by the trade-off between a high electromechanical coupling coefficient ($k^2$) for wide-band operation and the emergence of spurious acoustic modes that limit the resonators' inductive bandwidth. This work reports a spurious-free thickness-extensional (TE)-mode bulk acoustic wave (BAW) resonator in single-crystal lithium niobate (LN) based on a grounded-ring electrode architecture. The proposed structure is analyzed through simulation and experimentally validated using electrical characterization and laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV). The results show that the grounded ring modifies the effective boundary conditions of the acoustic device, enabling a piston-like modal response that suppresses lateral spurious modes across the inductive band. The demonstrated device operates at 10.14 MHz and achieves an electromechanical coupling coefficient of 29.6%, a maximum in-band Bode quality factor ($Q_\textit{Bode}$) of 5230, and a figure of merit (FoM, $Q\cdot k^2$) of 1548. These results establish the grounded-ring TE-mode LN BAW resonator as a practical platform for piezoelectric power conversion and a broader design approach for realizing high-performance spurious-free acoustic resonators.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Implicit DeepReach Without Implicit Differentiation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We consider the problem of approximating backward reachable and reach-avoid tubes for high-dimensional nonlinear systems whose Hamiltonians require numerical optimization over constrained controls and disturbances. Existing neural Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability methods alleviate the dimensionality bottleneck of grid-based solvers, but evaluating Hamiltonians without closed-form expressions introduces an additional computational challenge. We show that, under suitable assumptions, the gradients required for value-function training can be computed without differentiating through the inner optimization problem. Specifically, we establish an envelope-type gradient identity for the saddle point Hamiltonian, under which the optimal control and disturbance enter backpropagation as constants without gradient tracking. This enables end-to-end neural HJ reachability with numerically evaluated Hamiltonians while avoiding both solver unrolling and implicit differentiation. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed approach on nonlinear reachability and reach-avoid problems of different scales.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Pulsatile Endocrine Regulation with a Releasable Hormone Pool: Impulsive Feedback Model
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: An impulsive model of endocrine regulation equipped with frequency- and amplitude-modulated pulsatile feedback is extended to study the dynamical effects pertaining to limitations due to the releasable hormone pool. The model describes a three-hormone regulatory loop and is applicable to endocrine systems such as the reproductive, stress, and growth hormone axes. Conditions guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of a periodic solution with a single feedback-triggered impulse per period (a 1-cycle) are derived, together with monotonicity properties of its characteristics. An explicit Jacobian formula is obtained to assess local orbital stability. Model analysis demonstrates that a reduced hormone-pool replenishment rate produces a lower-amplitude, higher-frequency 1-cycle. This behavior is consistent with experimentally observed alterations in testosterone regulation in aging human males.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Force-Closure Condition for Cooperative Multi-robot Pushing of Rectangular Objects
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: In cooperative object manipulation, the placement of pushing contacts determines whether force closure can be achieved and agents can generate arbitrary forces and torques on the object correspondingly. This study derives a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for the planar force closure of a rectangular object, a common object shape in everyday settings, under four frictionless pushing contacts. For a rectangle of length $b$ and width $a$, force closure holds if and only if $(l_1+l_3-b)(l_2+l_4-a)<0$, where $l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4$ are the four edge contact locations. This condition is independent of the object's center of mass and is used to verify contact configurations before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of the two factors indicate which opposing contact pair should be adjusted. The condition and adjustment rule are then integrated into a full-pose trajectory-tracking framework as a geometric feasibility layer to demonstrate their use in control. Static wrench feasibility tests validate the proposed condition, while narrow-passage floating-body simulations show that maintaining a force-closure configuration reduces the RMS tracking errors in $x$, $y$, and unwrapped yaw from $12.05$ m, $18.11$ m, and $535.96^\circ$ to $2.24$ m, $2.66$ m, and $2.69^\circ$, respectively.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 7 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Published in CAOS 2026

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Image-Driven Control with Application to Thermoforming
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: This paper proposes Image-Driven Control (IDC), an approach to vision-based feedback that operates directly in the image space. IDC offers a direct end-to-end solution in the behavioral framework. Targeting a limited subset of vision-based feedback problems, including applications in manufacturing, the IDC design builds on a computationally advantageous subspace predictive control formulation and offset-free tracking to enable reference tracking in the image space under input and pixel-level constraints. IDC provides a control-theoretic alternative to vision-based feedback systems, enabling improved transparency for analysis and tuning of end-to-end control. It offers straightforward experiment design, an advantage in applications where data collection is expensive. The effectiveness of IDC is shown in a simulation example using a nonlinear high-fidelity model of the heating phase of the thermoforming process.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Presented at the 23rd IFAC World Congress (IFAC 2026), Busan, Republic of Korea, August 2026

Systems and Control (EESS).title: A Quantitative Approach to Reach-Avoid Reachability Analysis for Discrete-Time Nonlinear Control Systems
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: A reach-avoid specification requires a dynamical system to reach a target set of states while avoiding a failure set. Reachability analysis partitions the state space into parts starting from which the specification can be satisfied by following some control signal and those from which it cannot despite the best control effort. In this paper, we present a quantitative approach for reachability analysis to analyze the satisfaction of avoid and reach-avoid specifications for discrete-time nonlinear control systems. In such an approach, a value function assigns a value to each state that determines how robustly the system satisfies or violates the specification starting from it and following the optimal control signal. However, computing such a value function is difficult. Instead, our approach constructs discrete abstractions on which it performs value iteration to compute sound bounds on the desired value function. The resulting lower bound enables a sound under-approximation of the reach-avoid set (RAS) and, in the avoid case, a sound over-approximation of the backward reachable set (BRS). When the control set is finite, the upper bound additionally enables a sound over-approximation of the RAS and, in the avoid case, a sound under-approximation of the BRS. Moreover, the obtained bounds provide quantitative guarantees on safety margins and, in discounted reach-avoid problems, on safe target-reaching times. When the control set is finite, they also bound failure-reaching times. Our approach further refines the abstraction by splitting the grid cells that could not be classified as within or outside the BRS (or RAS) to improve the bounds. We evaluate our approach on five systems with up to five-dimensional state spaces.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Computing GR(1) Assume-Guarantee Contracts
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Assume-guarantee contracts provide a set of algebraic operations that enable the efficient compositional design and analysis of complex engineering systems. The explicit computation of these operations at component interfaces is currently supported only for some logics lacking a notion of time. This paper develops theory and algorithms to compute these operations when the contracts are expressed in the GR(1) modulo theory. The key challenge is the computation of two quantifier elimination problems for temporal formulas. We develop context-aided variable elimination procedures on GR(1)-modulo formulas, establish their soundness, characterize subproblem-wise optimal solutions within an admissible class of formulas, and use the procedures to compute contract operations, including composition and quotient. We implement the resulting framework in Pacti, automating compositional reasoning over GR(1) contracts. Finally, we demonstrate the framework on an automated emergency-braking case study, where we compute system-level contracts and expose compatibility conditions arising from the interaction of component specifications. Experiments on synthetic families show that the cost is governed by the number of eliminated variables and liveness conjuncts, and a comparison with exact automata-based elimination shows complementary scaling.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control for Underactuated Upright Physical Assistance
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), October 2026. 8 pages, 5 figures

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Robust State-Parameter Estimation in Second-Order Thévenin Batteries
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: We propose a scheme for estimating the full states and parameters of a second-order Thévenin battery model, using distinct features of the measured current. An identification step, run during suitable rest intervals, identifies the resistances and capacitances of the two RC branches from the voltage relaxation by linear least squares, without knowledge of the open-circuit voltage (OCV) map. An online estimator then runs continuously: the polarization voltages are estimated by open-loop observers; the series resistance is updated at current jumps using least squares; the state of charge (SOC) is propagated by Coulomb counting using the current capacity estimate, and both estimates are updated periodically by a sliding-window regression. We show that the identification is exact under a mild rank condition, that the series resistance is recovered at the first current jump, and that the online state and capacity estimates converge exponentially under verifiable excitation conditions. We also establish robustness of the online estimator under bounded process disturbances and measurement noise.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Under review for European Control Conference (ECC)

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Holonic Graceful Transitions Across Centralized, Decentralized, Distributed, and Local Control in DER-rich Cyber-Power Distribution System
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) in distribution system necessitates adaptive coordination frameworks. These frameworks must remain optimal during normal operation and resilient under cyber physical disturbances. Existing coordinated control approaches are typically deployed as static architectures with limited ability to adapt when communication degrades, local instability emerges, and operating conditions become spatially heterogeneous. This work addresses the gap by proposing a DER service-independent edge autonomous holonic adaptive coordination framework. In this framework, each DER controller executes its own control actions and transitions among centralized, distributed, decentralized, and local autonomous coordination modes without always relying on static coordination commands from the grid operator. The framework preserves coordination continuity across modes by retaining local controller states while reconfiguring only the coordination topology, information exchange pattern, and fallback action associated with the active DER service. Graceful transitions are enabled through dwell timers, rate limiting, and safety overrides to prevent dynamic instability during mode changes. Volt VAR control is used as a representative distribution automation application to validate the proposed architecture in a cyber-physical Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed. The proposed approach is evaluated under diverse cyber-physical event-based scenarios, showing region-confined adaptation under localized disturbance, reduced coordination traffic during coordination switching, and node-confined mitigation under cyber attack through edge anomaly detection and neighbor-corroborated impact estimation.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: Need full revision of the paper due to strong comments from reviewers

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Risk-Aware Dynamic Operating Envelopes for Battery Arbitrage in Unbalanced Distribution Networks
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs) provide network-aware limits for distributed energy resource scheduling while respecting network operating constraints. This paper develops a risk-aware DOE framework for battery arbitrage in unbalanced three-phase networks using a semidefinite program (SDP). We derive sufficient conditions for exactness of the SDP relaxation, ensuring that the recovered operating points satisfy all constraints of the original AC network model. The method computes hourly active-power DOEs under uncertain load conditions and incorporates them directly into a 24-hour battery arbitrage problem.On a modified IEEE 13-bus feeder, empirical comparisons with unconstrained arbitrage and local Volt--VAR/Volt--Watt control show that DOE-constrained scheduling eliminates the observed out-of-sample voltage violations while retaining 94.6% of the unconstrained arbitrage profit.
Systems and Control (EESS).comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Extended version of a manuscript prepared for the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Neural Network-Enhanced Frequency-Constrained Optimal Power Flow With Worst RoCoF and Frequency Deviation
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Frequency-constrained optimal power flow (FCOPF) should keep the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) and the frequency deviation (FD) within their limits after a specified generator out-age. The linearized frequency constraints commonly used in FCOPF are derived from aggregated system frequency response (SFR) models, which describe the center of inertia (COI) fre-quency with simplified governor dynamics and can underesti-mate the frequency excursions experienced by individual genera-tors. To address this issue, this paper develops a neural network-based frequency predictor (NN-FP) trained on electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations in PSCAD/EMTDC. The NN-FP predicts the worst RoCoF and the worst FD over the monitored generators, namely the generators at all buses other than the contingency bus. The trained NN-FP is reformulated and embed-ded into FCOPF with tightened frequency limits obtained from the test set prediction errors of NN-FP, leading to the proposed NN-FCOPF. The proposed model is compared with a traditional optimal power flow and a linearized FCOPF. EMT validation of 24-hour dispatches on the IEEE 9-bus and 39-bus systems shows that NN-FCOPF satisfies both limits in all hourly cases for the specified contingency, whereas the linearized FCOPF violates the limits in some hours because it underestimates the worst genera-tor RoCoF and FD.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Fast Sampling or High Gain? iP versus PI Control
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Intelligent proportional (iP) controllers, introduced in the framework of model-free control, are often presented as an alternative to proportional-integral (PI) controllers that requires no model of the plant. This paper studies this property for a first-order linear plant under sampled-data implementation with a zero-order hold. When the time derivative of the output is estimated by a backward difference, the discrete-time iP and PI controllers are known to obey the same control law under a one-to-one correspondence between their parameters. Building on this correspondence, the paper derives necessary and sufficient conditions for exponential stability of the iP closed loop, in closed form, in terms of the controller parameters KP and alpha, the sampling period h, and the plant parameters. It then shows that, when the iP parameters are held fixed and the sampling period tends to zero, the closed-loop decay rate tends to the iP gain KP, provided that KP is positive and that the ratio rho between the input gain of the plant and alpha satisfies 0 < rho < 2. One closed-loop pole then behaves as 1 - h KP, while the other tends to 1 - rho. With fixed PI gains, by contrast, the decay rate tends to that of the continuous-time PI loop, which depends on the plant parameters. The two parametrizations therefore suggest different tuning procedures, although they achieve the same closed loops at every fixed sampling period. High gain for the PI is, in some sense, replaced by fast sampling of the iP. The results also make explicit which plant information the iP controller requires: the sign of the input gain and a bound on its magnitude in the limit of fast sampling, and bounds on both plant parameters at a given sampling period. Numerical experiments illustrate these results.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

Systems and Control (EESS).title: Computationally Constrained First-Order Prediction-Correction Approach for Time-Varying Convex Optimization
Systems and Control (EESS).summary: Time-varying optimization methods often predict the locations of time-varying optima, then sample the objective function being minimized, and then compute corrections to those predictions.
